bw: Mineral required to make T3 and T4
Attaches to thyroglobulin in the colloid
tp: Thyroid hormone production depends on iodine, which attaches to thyroglobulin inside the follicle colloid.

ww.Calcium: Calcium is regulated by PTH and calcitonin and is not part of thyroid hormones.
ww.Iron: Iron is not a component of T3 or T4.

evidence: Hormones are produced in the colloid when atoms of the mineral iodine attach to a glycoprotein, called thyroglobulin, that is secreted into the colloid by the follicle cells.

bw: Glycoprotein secreted into the thyroid colloid
Iodine attaches to its tyrosine residues
tp: Follicle cells secrete thyroglobulin into the colloid, where iodinated tyrosines are linked to make T3 and T4.

ww.Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG): TBG is a plasma transport protein that carries T3 and T4 in the blood.
ww.Calcitonin: Calcitonin is a peptide hormone from the parafollicular cells.

evidence: Hormones are produced in the colloid when atoms of the mineral iodine attach to a glycoprotein, called thyroglobulin, that is secreted into the colloid by the follicle cells.

bw: The more commonly formed thyroid hormone
Cells convert it to the more potent T3
tp: T4 is formed far more often than T3, but T3 is more potent and many cells convert T4 into T3 by removing one iodine.

ww.Triiodothyronine (T3): T3 has three iodines and is the more potent product of T4 conversion.
ww.Calcitonin: Calcitonin is not an iodinated hormone.

evidence: Much more commonly, two copies of the second intermediary bond, forming tetraiodothyronine, also known as thyroxine (T4), a thyroid hormone with four iodines.

tp: T3 is more potent than T4, and many cells make it by removing an iodine atom from T4.

ww.Thyroxine (T4): T4 has four iodines and is less potent than T3.

evidence: T3 is more potent than T4, and many cells convert T4 to T3 through the removal of an iodine atom.

bw: Plasma protein that carries circulating T3 and T4
Holds about 99 percent of thyroid hormone bound in the blood
tp: Most circulating T3 and T4 is protein bound, which stops free diffusion into cells; only the small unbound fraction enters cells.

ww.Thyroglobulin: Thyroglobulin is the colloid protein inside thyroid follicles where hormone is made.
ww.Transferrin: Transferrin carries iron, not thyroid hormone.

evidence: The remaining 99 percent of circulating T3 and T4 is bound to specialized transport proteins called thyroxine-binding globulins (TBGs), to albumin, or to other plasma proteins.

bw: Hypothalamic hormone that triggers TSH secretion
tp: Low thyroid hormone stimulates TRH, which triggers TSH, which stimulates T3 and T4 release; rising T3 and T4 shut the axis down by negative feedback.

ww.Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH): CRH drives ACTH release and the adrenal axis.

evidence: As shown in Figure 17.13, low blood levels of T3 and T4 stimulate the release of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus, which triggers secretion of TSH from the anterior pituitary.

bw: Amount of energy the body uses at rest
tp: T3 and T4 are called metabolic hormones because they set basal metabolic rate by increasing nutrient breakdown and oxygen use.

ww.Glomerular filtration rate: GFR is the volume of filtrate formed by the kidneys, not the energy used at rest.
ww.Cardiac output: Cardiac output is blood pumped per minute, not resting energy use.

evidence: The thyroid hormones, T3 and T4, are often referred to as metabolic hormones because their levels influence the body’s basal metabolic rate, the amount of energy used by the body at rest.

bw: Inefficient ATP production releases extra heat
tp: T3 and T4 make ATP production inefficient, so extra heat is released, which raises body temperature.

ww.Diabetogenic effect: The diabetogenic effect is growth hormone raising blood glucose through liver glycogen breakdown.
ww.Glucose-sparing effect: The glucose-sparing effect is growth hormone driving lipolysis so tissues use fatty acids.

evidence: This so-called calorigenic effect (calor- = “heat”) raises body temperature.

tp: In Graves’ disease, antibodies overstimulate the thyroid follicle cells; they also inflame the orbital soft tissues, so the eyes can bulge.

ww.Hashimoto thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis destroys thyroid tissue and causes low thyroid hormone, not overstimulation.
ww.Hypoparathyroidism: Hypoparathyroidism is PTH deficiency with low blood calcium.

evidence: In Graves’ disease, the hyperthyroid state results from an autoimmune reaction in which antibodies overstimulate the follicle cells of the thyroid gland.

tp: When T3 and T4 cannot be made, TSH rises, colloid builds up and the thyroid enlarges. A goiter is only the visible sign of the deficiency.

ww.Exophthalmos: Exophthalmos is bulging of the eyes, seen with Graves’ disease.
ww.Acromegaly: Acromegaly is excess growth hormone in adults.

evidence: The accumulation of colloid increases the overall size of the thyroid gland, a condition called a goiter (Figure 17.14).

bw: Primary cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide
Mineral lacking in the diet of many landlocked regions
tp: Iodine deficiency impairs T3 and T4 synthesis. Iodized salt is the main dietary source in many countries.

ww.Vitamin D deficiency: The source ties preventable intellectual disability to iodine, not vitamin D.
ww.Vitamin C deficiency: Vitamin C deficiency is not linked to thyroid hormone synthesis.

evidence: Moreover, iodine deficiency is the primary cause of preventable intellectual disabilies worldwide.

tp: Low thyroid hormone lowers metabolic rate. Where iodine is available, inflammation of the thyroid is the more common cause.

ww.Hyperthyroidism: Hyperthyroidism raises metabolic rate and causes weight loss, heat intolerance and diarrhea.
ww.Hyperparathyroidism: Hyperparathyroidism is PTH excess, which lowers bone density.

evidence: Called hypothyroidism, the condition is characterized by a low metabolic rate, weight gain, cold extremities, constipation, reduced libido, menstrual irregularities, and reduced mental activity.

bw: Weight loss, tremors, increased heart rate
tp: Elevated thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate. It is often caused by a pituitary or thyroid tumor, or by Graves’ disease.

ww.Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism gives weight gain, cold extremities and slowed activity.
ww.Hypoparathyroidism: Hypoparathyroidism gives low calcium with muscle cramping and spasms.

evidence: Hyperthyroidism can lead to an increased metabolic rate, excessive body heat and sweating, diarrhea, weight loss, tremors, and increased heart rate.

bw: Secreted by parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid
tp: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, boosting osteoblast activity, reducing intestinal absorption and increasing urinary loss, though its role in calcium homeostasis is minor.

ww.Parathyroid hormone (PTH): PTH is released when calcium is low and raises blood calcium.
ww.Calcitriol: Calcitriol is made in the kidney and increases intestinal calcium absorption.

evidence: The thyroid gland also secretes a hormone called calcitonin that is produced by the parafollicular cells (also called C cells) that stud the tissue between distinct follicles.

bw: Greater sensitivity to epinephrine and norepinephrine
ans: Faster heart rate and higher blood pressure
d: Slower heart rate and lower blood pressure
Lower body temperature with weight gain
tp: Thyroid hormones upregulate catecholamine receptors in blood vessels. In excess this accelerates the heart rate, strengthens the heartbeat and raises blood pressure.

ww.Slower heart rate and lower blood pressu: Excess thyroid hormone does the opposite and speeds the heart.
ww.Lower body temperature with weight gain: Excess thyroid hormone raises heat production and metabolic rate.

evidence: When levels of T3 and T4 hormones are excessive, this effect accelerates the heart rate, strengthens the heartbeat, and increases blood pressure.
